cards.note: Genesis 30:18 — *And Leah said, Elohim (God) hath given me my hire, because I have given my maiden to my husband: and she called his name Issachar.* *And Jacob knew Leah, and she 'conceived and' bare me, and on account of the hire I was called Issachar.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 62:15) Genesis gives the reason for the name in Leah's own mouth, and the Testament of Issachar has the son say the same thing back: "on account of the hire I was called Issachar." The name is a receipt for the night Leah paid for.
cards.member_note: Genesis 30:18 — *Elohim (God) hath given me my hire … and she called his name Issachar.* The name Issachar is tied to the hire Leah paid, and the Testament of Issachar says the same.

cards.note: Genesis 30:14 — *And Reuben went in the days of wheat harvest, and found mandrakes in the field, and brought them unto his mother Leah. Then Rachel said to Leah, Give me, I pray thee, of thy son’s mandrakes.* *For Reuben 'my brother' brought in mandrakes from the field, and Rachel met him and took them.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 62:3) Genesis puts Reuben in the field in the days of wheat harvest and has Rachel ask Leah for the mandrakes, while the Testament of Issachar has Rachel meet him and take them. The two tellings agree on where the quarrel between the sisters began.
cards.member_note: Genesis 30:14 — *Rachel said to Leah, Give me, I pray thee, of thy son’s mandrakes.* Reuben brings the mandrakes home and the sisters' quarrel begins, in Genesis as in the Testament of Issachar.

cards.note: Genesis 30:16 — *And Jacob came out of the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him, and said, Thou must come in unto me; for surely I have hired thee with my son’s mandrakes. And he lay with her that night.* *Nevertheless, for the mandrakes I am hiring Jacob to thee for one night.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 62:14) Both tellings call the night a purchase: Genesis has Leah say she had hired Jacob with her son's mandrakes, and the Testament of Issachar has Rachel say "I am hiring Jacob to thee for one night." The Testament only changes who is speaking.
cards.member_note: Genesis 30:16 — *I have hired thee with my son’s mandrakes.* Jacob's night with Leah is bargained for with mandrakes, just as the Testament of Issachar says.

cards.note: Genesis 29:25 — *And it came to pass, that in the morning, behold, it was Leah: and he said to Laban, What is this thou hast done unto me? did not I serve with thee for Rachel? wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?* *For thou art not his wife, but in craft wert taken to him in my stead.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 62:12) Rachel's complaint in the Testament of Issachar, that Leah was taken to Jacob "in craft," is the very thing Jacob says to Laban the morning after: "wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?" Laban's trick lies underneath the whole quarrel over the mandrakes.
cards.member_note: Genesis 29:25 — *wherefore then hast thou beguiled me.* Laban's deception, the root of the sisters' rivalry, is what the Testament of Issachar calls craft.

thread.title: Hired for the mandrakes — how Issachar got his name
thread.summary_md:
It ain't new, because the Testament of Issachar opens with a scene Genesis had already told, and lets the son tell it from his own side, beginning with his birth.

*I was born the 'fifth son to Jacob', by way of hire for the mandrakes.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 62:2)

Genesis shows where the mandrakes came from and who wanted them, and the bargain that followed is the same in both tellings, one night with Jacob paid for in mandrakes.

*And Reuben went in the days of wheat harvest, and found mandrakes in the field, and brought them unto his mother Leah. Then Rachel said to Leah, Give me, I pray thee, of thy son’s mandrakes.* (Genesis 30:14)

*And Jacob came out of the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him, and said, Thou must come in unto me; for surely I have hired thee with my son’s mandrakes. And he lay with her that night.* (Genesis 30:16)

*Nevertheless, for the mandrakes I am hiring Jacob to thee for one night.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 62:14)

The name came out of that bargain, and Leah gives the reason in Genesis just as the son repeats it in the Testament.

*And Leah said, Elohim (God) hath given me my hire, because I have given my maiden to my husband: and she called his name Issachar.* (Genesis 30:18)

*And Jacob knew Leah, and she 'conceived and' bare me, and on account of the hire I was called Issachar.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 62:15)

Underneath it lies the wrong done to both sisters, which Rachel names bitterly in the Testament and which Jacob names in Genesis the morning he finds Leah beside him.

*For thou art not his wife, but in craft wert taken to him in my stead.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 62:12)

*And it came to pass, that in the morning, behold, it was Leah: and he said to Laban, What is this thou hast done unto me? did not I serve with thee for Rachel? wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?* (Genesis 29:25)

So the reader is handed no new story but an old one told by a son who remembers how his name was bought. The Testament adds small details, yet the field, the mandrakes, the night, the hire and the name all stand where Genesis put them.

chapters.flag: Retelling stays close to Genesis 29 and 30; the added details (apples in Haran, the speeches) are the Testament's own and no doctrine is built on them.

cards.note: Genesis 30:22 — *And Elohim (God) remembered Rachel, and Elohim (God) hearkened to her, and opened her womb.* *For on the morrow also she again gave up Jacob. Because of the mandrakes, therefore, Yahuah (Lord) hearkened to Rachel.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 63:4) Genesis says Elohim (God) remembered Rachel and hearkened to her, and the Testament of Issachar says the very same of Yahuah (the Lord): He hearkened to Rachel. The mandrakes are not the point; the hearing is.
cards.member_note: Genesis 30:22 — *And Elohim (God) remembered Rachel, and Elohim (God) hearkened to her, and opened her womb.* Rachel is heard and her womb is opened, in Genesis and in the Testament of Issachar.

cards.note: Genesis 30:23 — *And she conceived, and bare a son; and said, Elohim (God) hath taken away my reproach:* *For He knew that for the sake of children she wished to company with Jacob, and not for lust of pleasure.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 63:3) The Testament of Issachar says Rachel wished for children and "not for lust of pleasure," and Genesis shows what she was really carrying: the reproach of barrenness, which Elohim (God) took away when Joseph was born.
cards.member_note: Genesis 30:23 — *Elohim (God) hath taken away my reproach.* What Rachel longed for was a son and an end to her reproach, as the Testament of Issachar says.

cards.note: Genesis 30:24 — *And she called his name Joseph; and said, Yahuah (LORD) shall add to me another son.* *Then appeared to Jacob an angel of Yahuah (Lord), saying: Two children shall Rachel bear, inasmuch as she hath refused company with her husband, and hath chosen continency.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 63:1) When the Testament of Issachar has an angel tell Jacob that Rachel shall bear "Two children," it is looking at the same hope Rachel voices at Joseph's birth, a second son to follow the first. Genesis does not mention the angel, so the reader should set the angel's word beside Rachel's and let Genesis stand as the record.
cards.member_note: Genesis 30:24 — *Yahuah (LORD) shall add to me another son.* Rachel asks Yahuah (the LORD) for one more son, which the Testament of Issachar reads as two children in all.

cards.note: Genesis 14:18 — *And Melek Tsadiq (Melchizedek) king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the El Elyon (most high God).* *For though she desired them, she eat them not, but offered them in the house of Yahuah (Lord), presenting them to the priest of the El Elyon (Most High) who was at that time.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 63:5) The Testament of Issachar says Rachel offered the mandrakes in the house of Yahuah (the Lord) to the priest of the El Elyon (Most High) of that time. Genesis does tell of Melek Tsadiq (Melchizedek) as priest of the El Elyon (most high God) in the days of Abraham, but nowhere says that mandrakes were brought to any priest, so the reader has Genesis for the priest and the Testament for the offering and no more than that.
cards.member_note: Genesis 14:18 — *priest of the El Elyon (most high God).* Genesis names a priest of the El Elyon (most high God) in the patriarchs' own time; the mandrake offering is the Testament's alone.

thread.title: Yahuah hearkened to Rachel — she was heard, and bare two sons
thread.summary_md:
It ain't new that the barren were heard, for Genesis said it of Rachel and the Testament of Issachar says it again in its own words, telling how Yahuah (the Lord) answered the sister who gave up her night.

*For on the morrow also she again gave up Jacob. Because of the mandrakes, therefore, Yahuah (Lord) hearkened to Rachel.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 63:4)

Genesis puts the answer plainly and leaves the mandrakes out of it.

*And Elohim (God) remembered Rachel, and Elohim (God) hearkened to her, and opened her womb.* (Genesis 30:22)

The Testament also says Rachel wanted children and not pleasure, and Genesis shows the want underneath it in her own cry when the son came.

*For He knew that for the sake of children she wished to company with Jacob, and not for lust of pleasure.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 63:3)

*And she conceived, and bare a son; and said, Elohim (God) hath taken away my reproach:* (Genesis 30:23)

The Testament then has an angel promise the two sons she would bear, while in Genesis her words at Joseph's birth already look ahead to a second.

*Then appeared to Jacob an angel of Yahuah (Lord), saying: Two children shall Rachel bear, inasmuch as she hath refused company with her husband, and hath chosen continency.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 63:1)

*And she called his name Joseph; and said, Yahuah (LORD) shall add to me another son.* (Genesis 30:24)

The reader should notice where the Testament goes beyond Genesis, since it brings an angel to Jacob and carries the mandrakes into the house of Yahuah (the Lord) to a priest of the El Elyon (Most High), and Genesis says nothing of either. The scripture beside it is the record of what was heard: a woman asked, Elohim (God) hearkened, and her reproach was taken away. That is enough to stand on without building anything on the additions.

chapters.flag: 63:1 (angel to Jacob) and 63:5 (mandrakes offered at the house of Yahuah to the priest of El Elyon) are not in Genesis; the house of Yahuah did not yet exist in Rachel's day. Set beside Genesis 30 and 14 only; nothing built on them.

cards.note: Proverbs 14:29 — *He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly.* *For anger is an evil thing, my children, for it troubleth even the soul itself.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 81:1) The Testament of Dan says anger "troubleth even the soul itself," and Proverbs says the same from the other side: the man quick to wrath is the one who lifts folly high. Both begin with what anger does to the man who carries it.
cards.member_note: Proverbs 14:29 — *he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly.* Quickness to wrath is folly, as the Testament of Dan says of the angry soul.

cards.note: James 1:20 — *For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of Elohim (God).* *And when the body does all these things, the soul justifieth what is done, since it seeth not aright.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 81:3) The Testament of Dan says the soul of an angry man "justifieth what is done, since it seeth not aright." James answers that wrath cannot produce the righteousness Elohim (God) asks for, however right it feels to the one who is angry.
cards.member_note: James 1:20 — *the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of Elohim (God).* Anger persuades the angry man that he is right, but it never makes him so.

cards.note: Proverbs 29:22 — *An angry man stirreth up strife, and a furious man aboundeth in transgression.* *And though the wrathful man be weak, yet hath he a power twofold of that which is by nature; for wrath ever aideth such in lawlessness.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 81:5) The Testament of Dan says wrath "ever aideth such in lawlessness," and Proverbs says that a furious man aboundeth in transgression. The two lines are one observation: anger multiplies sin.
cards.member_note: Proverbs 29:22 — *a furious man aboundeth in transgression.* Anger feeds on itself and abounds in transgression, as the Testament of Dan teaches.

cards.note: Ephesians 4:27 — *Neither give place to the devil.* *This spirit goeth always with lying 'at the right hand of Satan, that with cruelty and lying' his works may be wrought.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 81:6) The Testament of Dan joins anger to lying and puts both at the right hand of Satan. The short line in Ephesians gives the same warning in a few words, that anger can open a door.
cards.member_note: Ephesians 4:27 — *Neither give place to the devil.* Anger is a door that must not be left open, a warning the Testament of Dan also gives.

thread.title: Anger troubles the soul, blinds it, and gives the devil a place
thread.summary_md:
It ain't new. Dan's warning about anger runs along lines the scriptures had already drawn, and in the Testament of Dan he speaks it as a dying father who knows what anger does to the one who carries it.

*For anger is an evil thing, my children, for it troubleth even the soul itself.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 81:1)

Proverbs had already named the folly of the hasty spirit, and Dan goes on to show how that folly reasons with itself, with the body doing the deed and the soul calling it just.

*He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly.* (Proverbs 14:29)

*And when the body does all these things, the soul justifieth what is done, since it seeth not aright.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 81:3)

James takes away that comfort in a single line, since however right wrath feels to the angry man it cannot work what Elohim (God) calls righteous.

*For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of Elohim (God).* (James 1:20)

Dan adds that wrath helps the strong and the weak alike toward lawlessness, which is what Proverbs means when it says a furious man aboundeth in transgression.

*And though the wrathful man be weak, yet hath he a power twofold of that which is by nature; for wrath ever aideth such in lawlessness.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 81:5)

*An angry man stirreth up strife, and a furious man aboundeth in transgression.* (Proverbs 29:22)

Last, Dan sets wrath beside lying at the right hand of Satan, and Ephesians gives a short warning against leaving the devil any place.

*This spirit goeth always with lying 'at the right hand of Satan, that with cruelty and lying' his works may be wrought.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 81:6)

*Neither give place to the devil.* (Ephesians 4:27)

None of this teaches that the commandments are loosened or that a man may be angry and call it righteous. It teaches that anger is a way off the path and a road into lawlessness, and that the one walking it is the last to see it, which is why a father warns his children while they can still turn.

cards.note: Deuteronomy 32:18 — *Of the Rock that begat thee thou art unmindful, and hast forgotten Elohim (God) that formed thee.* *[Nevertheless, 'Dan' prophesied unto them that they should forget their Elohim (God), and should be alienated from the land of their inheritance 'and from the race of Israel', and from the family of 'their seed'.]* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 85:3) The Testament of Dan says his sons "should forget their Elohim (God)," and Moses had already put that charge in a song: Yashar'el (Israel) forgot Elohim (God) who formed them. The bracketed sentence is Dan's sorrow, and the song is Moses' warning.
cards.member_note: Deuteronomy 32:18 — *hast forgotten Elohim (God) that formed thee.* Forgetting Elohim (God) is the old charge in Moses' song, and the Testament of Dan repeats it over his own tribe.

cards.note: Judges 18:30 — *And the children of Dan set up the graven image: and Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh, he and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land.* *[Nevertheless, 'Dan' prophesied unto them that they should forget their Elohim (God), and should be alienated from the land of their inheritance 'and from the race of Israel', and from the family of 'their seed'.]* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 85:3) Scripture records how the tribe of Dan set up a graven image for itself and kept priests for it until the day of the captivity of the land. This is the scripture beside the Testament of Dan's saying that his sons would be "alienated from the land of their inheritance." The sentence in the Testament is bracketed in the translation, so the reader should let Judges stand as the witness.
cards.member_note: Judges 18:30 — *the children of Dan set up the graven image.* Dan's turning aside to an image is told in Judges and lies behind the Testament of Dan's foretelling.

cards.note: Genesis 49:31 — *There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife; there they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife; and there I buried Leah.* *And his sons buried him. And after that they carried up 'his bones', and placed them near Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 85:2) The Testament of Dan says his sons carried up his bones and "placed them near Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob." Genesis names the cave where Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah were buried, which is the burying place the fathers' sons were laid beside. It does not say where Dan was buried, so the Testament speaks for itself there.
cards.member_note: Genesis 49:31 — *There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife.* Genesis names the patriarchs' burying place, beside which the Testament of Dan says Dan was laid.

thread.title: Dan buried near his fathers — yet his sons forget Elohim and are alienated from the land
thread.summary_md:
The Testament of Dan ends with a burial and a sorrow, for his sons lay his bones near the fathers, and then the text adds a prophecy, set in brackets by the translator, of what would come on his seed.

*And his sons buried him. And after that they carried up 'his bones', and placed them near Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 85:2)

*[Nevertheless, 'Dan' prophesied unto them that they should forget their Elohim (God), and should be alienated from the land of their inheritance 'and from the race of Israel', and from the family of 'their seed'.]* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 85:3)

It ain't new that the scripture said this about Dan, because Moses had already told Yashar'el (Israel) in his song what forgetting looks like, and the book of Judges records how Dan's own children set up their image and kept it until the land went into captivity.

*Of the Rock that begat thee thou art unmindful, and hast forgotten Elohim (God) that formed thee.* (Deuteronomy 32:18)

*And the children of Dan set up the graven image: and Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh, he and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land.* (Judges 18:30)

The burying place the Testament names is the one Genesis names, the cave Jacob spoke of as his sons gathered, where Abraham and Sarah lay and Isaac and Rebekah after them.

*There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife; there they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife; and there I buried Leah.* (Genesis 49:31)

So the Testament of Dan lays Dan beside the fathers and in the same breath grieves that his seed would be separated from the land and from the race of Yashar'el (Israel). That grief is no new teaching, because Moses foretold the forgetting and the later books show it coming true. The bracketed sentence should be held lightly, and the burying place and the song held firmly.

chapters.flag: 85:3 is bracketed by the translator as an interpolation; set beside Deuteronomy and Judges only. The Testament puts Dan's bones near the fathers, while Acts 7:16 speaks of the fathers laid at Sychem; not harmonized here. Summary's last sentence leans on Moses' gathering promise (Deut 30) which is not quoted in the files used; kept as a general statement.

cards.note: Genesis 45:28 — *And Yashar'el (Israel) said, It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive: I will go and see him before I die.* *Then my father saith unto me: I believe Elohim (God) that Joseph liveth, for I see 'always' that Yahuah (Lord) numbereth him with you.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 92:2) In the Testament of Naphtali, Jacob says he believes Elohim (God) that Joseph lives, and when the news finally comes in Genesis the old man says it plainly: "Joseph my son is yet alive." What he held in hope the wagons made certain.
cards.member_note: Genesis 45:28 — *Joseph my son is yet alive.* Jacob's faith that Joseph lives, in the Testament of Naphtali, becomes his plain word in Genesis.

cards.note: Genesis 37:11 — *And his brethren envied him; but his father observed the saying.* *These two dreams I told to my father; and he said to me: These things must be fulfilled in their season, after that Yashar'el (Israel) hath endured many things.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 92:1) Joseph's father in Genesis "observed the saying" of the dreams, and in the Testament of Naphtali he tells his son the dreams must be fulfilled in their season, after Yashar'el (Israel) has endured many things. Both show a father who kept the dreams in mind.
cards.member_note: Genesis 37:11 — *And his brethren envied him; but his father observed the saying.* Jacob did not forget Joseph's dreams, as Genesis and the Testament of Naphtali both show.

cards.note: Genesis 37:35 — *And all his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him; but he refused to be comforted; and he said, For I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning. Thus his father wept for him.* *And he said, weeping: Ah me, my son, Joseph, thou livest, though I behold thee not, and thou seest not Jacob that begat thee.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 92:3) Genesis tells that Jacob refused comfort and said he would go down mourning to the grave, and the Testament of Naphtali has him weeping, "Ah me, my son, Joseph, thou livest, though I behold thee not." The tears are the same; the Testament adds that his hope was alive under them.
cards.member_note: Genesis 37:35 — *but he refused to be comforted; and he said, For I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning.* Jacob's mourning for Joseph, the weeping in the Testament of Naphtali, is the same grief Genesis records.

cards.note: Genesis 37:33 — *And he knew it, and said, It is my son’s coat; an evil beast hath devoured him; Joseph is without doubt rent in pieces.* *He caused me also, therefore, to weep by these words, and I burned in my heart to declare that 'Joseph' had been sold, but I feared my brethren.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 92:4) Naphtali confesses he burned to declare that Joseph had been sold, but feared his brethren. Genesis shows what the silence cost, for Jacob looked at the coat and cried that Joseph was without doubt rent in pieces.
cards.member_note: Genesis 37:33 — *an evil beast hath devoured him.* The brothers' silence let Jacob believe a lie, and the Testament of Naphtali says one of them longed to speak.

thread.title: I believe Elohim that Joseph liveth — Jacob's hope and Naphtali's silence
thread.summary_md:
Naphtali tells his sons of two dreams of Joseph and of the answer his father gave him, and Genesis agrees that Jacob did not forget such dreams.

*These two dreams I told to my father; and he said to me: These things must be fulfilled in their season, after that Yashar'el (Israel) hath endured many things.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 92:1)

*And his brethren envied him; but his father observed the saying.* (Genesis 37:11)

The Testament then shows what Jacob held on to long after the coat was brought, and Genesis keeps both sides of the old man in view, his refusal of comfort and his word when the news came.

*Then my father saith unto me: I believe Elohim (God) that Joseph liveth, for I see 'always' that Yahuah (Lord) numbereth him with you.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 92:2)

*And he said, weeping: Ah me, my son, Joseph, thou livest, though I behold thee not, and thou seest not Jacob that begat thee.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 92:3)

*And all his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him; but he refused to be comforted; and he said, For I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning. Thus his father wept for him.* (Genesis 37:35)

*And Yashar'el (Israel) said, It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive: I will go and see him before I die.* (Genesis 45:28)

Naphtali confesses his own part, and Genesis shows the quiet cost of it, since the father said what he supposed was true.

*He caused me also, therefore, to weep by these words, and I burned in my heart to declare that 'Joseph' had been sold, but I feared my brethren.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 92:4)

*And he knew it, and said, It is my son’s coat; an evil beast hath devoured him; Joseph is without doubt rent in pieces.* (Genesis 37:33)

It ain't new that Jacob grieved and that the brothers kept silent. What the Testament adds is a father who half believed his son still lived and a son who feared to tell him. The two do not agree in every detail, since Genesis shows Jacob's heart faint when first told that Joseph lived, so Genesis is the record and the Testament a father's hope remembered by a son.

chapters.flag: 92:2-3: Jacob believing Joseph lives is not in Genesis, which has him mourning till the wagons come (Gen 45:26-28); the Testament's version is set beside, not harmonized.

cards.note: Genesis 49:29 — *And he charged them, and said unto them, I am to be gathered unto my people: bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite,* *And when he had charged them with many such words, he exhorted them that they should remove his bones to Hebron, and that they should bury him with his fathers.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 94:1) Naphtali charges his sons to bury him with his fathers, as Jacob had charged his own. The Testament of Naphtali and Genesis speak with one voice at the deathbed: a patriarch who wishes to lie with his people.
cards.member_note: Genesis 49:29 — *bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite* A dying patriarch asks to be buried with his fathers, as Jacob did in Genesis and Naphtali does in his Testament.

cards.note: Genesis 23:19 — *And after this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre: the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan.* *And when he had charged them with many such words, he exhorted them that they should remove his bones to Hebron, and that they should bury him with his fathers.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 94:1) The Testament of Naphtali names Hebron as the place for his bones, and Genesis is where Hebron first becomes a burying place, when Abraham buried Sarah there. The fathers' graves are the reason Naphtali asks to be taken there.
cards.member_note: Genesis 23:19 — *the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan.* Abraham buried Sarah at Hebron, the cave to which Naphtali asks to be carried.

cards.note: Genesis 49:33 — *And when Jacob had made an end of commanding his sons, he gathered up his feet into the bed, and yielded up the ghost, and was gathered unto his people.* *And when he had eaten and drunken with a merry heart, he covered his face and died.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 94:2) The Testament of Naphtali says he "covered his face and died," and Genesis closes Jacob's life with the same plainness: he gathered up his feet and was gathered to his people. In both, a father finishes his commands and then departs.
cards.member_note: Genesis 49:33 — *and yielded up the ghost, and was gathered unto his people.* Naphtali ends his charge and dies like Jacob, gathered to his people.

cards.note: Genesis 50:12 — *And his sons did unto him according as he commanded them:* *And his sons did according to all that Naphtali their father had commanded them.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 94:3) The Testament of Naphtali says his sons "did according to all that Naphtali their father had commanded them." Genesis has the very same obedience from Jacob's sons when they buried their father.
cards.member_note: Genesis 50:12 — *his sons did unto him according as he commanded them.* Sons who carry out a dying father's command are the picture in both Genesis and the Testament of Naphtali.

cards.note: Genesis 25:8 — *Then Abraham gave up the ghost, and died in a good old age, an old man, and full of years; and was gathered to his people.* *And when he had said these things unto them, he commanded saying: Bury me in Hebron. And he fell asleep and died at a good old age.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 110:1) Asher falls asleep "at a good old age," the same words Genesis uses of Abraham. Both end full of days and gathered to their people.
cards.member_note: Genesis 25:8 — *died in a good old age.* Asher's end in the Testament of Asher is told in the words used of Abraham.

cards.note: Genesis 49:31 — *There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife; there they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife; and there I buried Leah.* *And when he had said these things unto them, he commanded saying: Bury me in Hebron. And he fell asleep and died at a good old age.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 110:1) Asher's command, "Bury me in Hebron," asks for the place where Genesis says Abraham and Sarah lay, and Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah. The fathers' burying place is what his request is aimed at.
cards.member_note: Genesis 49:31 — *There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife.* Hebron holds the fathers' graves, which is why Asher asks to be carried there.

cards.note: Genesis 50:13 — *For his sons carried him into the land of Canaan, and buried him in the cave of the field of Machpelah, which Abraham bought with the field for a possession of a buryingplace of Ephron the Hittite, before Mamre.* *And his sons did as he had commanded them, and they carried him up to Hebron, and buried him with his fathers.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 110:2) The sons of Asher "carried him up to Hebron, and buried him with his fathers," and Genesis tells how Jacob's sons carried their father to the same cave of Machpelah. The Testament of Asher closes with the same obedience.
cards.member_note: Genesis 50:13 — *his sons carried him into the land of Canaan.* Jacob's sons carried him to Machpelah just as Asher's sons carry him to Hebron.

cards.note: Genesis 39:9 — *There is none greater in this house than I; neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against Elohim (God)?* *I therefore, when I heard this, rent my garments, and said unto her: Woman, reverence Elohim (God), and do not this evil deed, lest thou be destroyed; for know indeed that I will declare this thy device unto all men.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 115:2) Joseph in the Testament of Joseph tells the woman to "reverence Elohim (God)" and refuse this evil deed, and in Genesis his refusal turns on the same fear: how can he do this great wickedness and sin against Elohim (God)? The sin is first against Elohim (God), and only then against the master.
cards.member_note: Genesis 39:9 — *how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against Elohim (God).* Joseph refuses on account of Elohim (God), in Genesis and in the Testament of Joseph alike.

cards.note: Exodus 20:14 — *Thou shalt not commit adultery.* *'And' again, at another time she said unto me: If thou wilt not commit adultery, I will kill my husband by poison, and take thee to be my husband.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 115:1) The woman's threat to kill her husband by poison so that she may take Joseph is a plot against this commandment from the start, and Joseph's answer in the Testament of Joseph is to refuse adultery. The commandment is the ground he stands on.
cards.member_note: Exodus 20:14 — *Thou shalt not commit adultery.* The commandment against adultery is what the woman asks Joseph to break and what he keeps.

cards.note: Proverbs 6:26 — *For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life.* *'And' again, at another time she said unto me: If thou wilt not commit adultery, I will kill my husband by poison, and take thee to be my husband.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 115:1) The Testament of Joseph has the woman offer to poison her husband, which shows how the adulteress "will hunt for the precious life" in Proverbs. The proverb warns a young man of exactly this woman.
cards.member_note: Proverbs 6:26 — *the adulteress will hunt for the precious life.* Proverbs warns that the adulteress hunts for a man's life, as the woman in the Testament of Joseph does.

cards.note: Proverbs 7:21 — *With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him.* *And she departed, soothing me with gifts, and sending to me every delight of the sons of men.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 115:4) When Joseph refuses, she goes away "soothing me with gifts," and the Proverbs describe how fair speech and flattering lips have forced the simple to yield. The gifts are the same snare as the fair words.
cards.member_note: Proverbs 7:21 — *With her much fair speech she caused him to yield.* Gifts and flattery are the adulteress's snares, in the Testament of Joseph and in Proverbs.

thread.title: Woman, reverence Elohim — Joseph refuses the threat of poison and the offer of gifts
thread.summary_md:
It ain't new. The temptation Joseph tells his sons about is the one Genesis records, and the commandment he stands on was given before either of them, so that the woman's offer is a breaking of the seventh commandment even as she plans to kill for it.

*'And' again, at another time she said unto me: If thou wilt not commit adultery, I will kill my husband by poison, and take thee to be my husband.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 115:1)

*Thou shalt not commit adultery.* (Exodus 20:14)

Proverbs warned that such a woman hunts for more than a night, and Joseph meets her by telling her whom to fear.

*For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life.* (Proverbs 6:26)

*I therefore, when I heard this, rent my garments, and said unto her: Woman, reverence Elohim (God), and do not this evil deed, lest thou be destroyed; for know indeed that I will declare this thy device unto all men.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 115:2)

Genesis says the same in a single sentence, grounding the refusal in Elohim (God) before it is grounded in loyalty to a master.

*There is none greater in this house than I; neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against Elohim (God)?* (Genesis 39:9)

When her threat fails she turns to kindness and gifts, and Proverbs describes what that kind of kindness is meant to do.

*And she departed, soothing me with gifts, and sending to me every delight of the sons of men.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 115:4)

*With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him.* (Proverbs 7:21)

The Testament of Joseph adds a poison plot and an offer of gifts that Genesis does not record, and the reader should keep those as Joseph's own telling. What stands firm is the pattern: the commandment given at Sinai, the warning given in Proverbs, and a young man who answers temptation with the fear of Elohim (God) and does not move. That is Torah lived, not a clever escape from it.

chapters.flag: Poison threat and gifts (115:1, 115:4) are the Testament's additions to Genesis 39; set beside Torah and Proverbs only.

cards.note: Genesis 39:10 — *And it came to pass, as she spake to Joseph day by day, that he hearkened not unto her, to lie by her, or to be with her.* *Then accordingly seizing an opportunity she rushed unto me while her husband was yet without, and said unto me: I will hang myself, or cast myself over a cliff, if thou wilt not lie with me.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 117:3) Genesis says the woman spoke to Joseph "day by day," and the Testament of Joseph shows what that daily pressure looked like when it grew desperate, with threats to hang herself or cast herself over a cliff. In both, Joseph does not hearken.
cards.member_note: Genesis 39:10 — *as she spake to Joseph day by day, that he hearkened not unto her* Day after day she pressed him, and Joseph would not listen, in Genesis and in the Testament of Joseph.

cards.note: Genesis 39:8 — *But he refused, and said unto his master’s wife, Behold, my master wotteth not what is with me in the house, and he hath committed all that he hath to my hand;* *But she knew not that because of my lord I spake thus, and not because of her.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 117:7) The Testament of Joseph says "because of my lord I spake thus, and not because of her," and Genesis gives Joseph's plea to the woman in the same spirit: his master had trusted him with all that he had. His loyalty was to the man who trusted him.
cards.member_note: Genesis 39:8 — *my master wotteth not what is with me in the house.* Joseph answers out of faithfulness to his master, which the Testament of Joseph puts as speaking because of his lord.

cards.note: Proverbs 5:22 — *His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be holden with the cords of his sins.* *For if a man hath fallen before the passion of a wicked desire and become enslaved by it, even as she, whatever good thing he may hear with regard to that passion, he receiveth it with a view to his wicked desire.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 117:8) The Testament of Joseph says that a man who has "become enslaved" to a wicked desire hears every good word as a help to that desire. Proverbs says the same of the wicked: his own iniquities take him and he is held with the cords of his sins.
cards.member_note: Proverbs 5:22 — *he shall be holden with the cords of his sins.* A man bound by his own desire is held by it, as the Testament of Joseph and Proverbs both say.

thread.title: The woman pleads and threatens, Joseph answers in faithfulness — and the cords of desire
thread.summary_md:
The Testament of Joseph tells the pressure in more detail than Genesis does, for the woman is done with subtlety, and Genesis keeps it short by saying she spoke to him day by day.

*Then accordingly seizing an opportunity she rushed unto me while her husband was yet without, and said unto me: I will hang myself, or cast myself over a cliff, if thou wilt not lie with me.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 117:3)

*And it came to pass, as she spake to Joseph day by day, that he hearkened not unto her, to lie by her, or to be with her.* (Genesis 39:10)

It ain't new that she kept at it, and the Testament simply opens the door a little wider on what those days were. Joseph's answer in the Testament tells whom he was serving, and Genesis gives the reason he gave her himself.

*But she knew not that because of my lord I spake thus, and not because of her.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 117:7)

*But he refused, and said unto his master’s wife, Behold, my master wotteth not what is with me in the house, and he hath committed all that he hath to my hand;* (Genesis 39:8)

The Testament adds a thought about the woman's state, that one given over to desire turns every wise word into fuel for it, and Proverbs describes the same trap from the outside.

*For if a man hath fallen before the passion of a wicked desire and become enslaved by it, even as she, whatever good thing he may hear with regard to that passion, he receiveth it with a view to his wicked desire.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 117:8)

*His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be holden with the cords of his sins.* (Proverbs 5:22)

The woman is bound by her own cords, and Joseph is free because he would not take hold of them. The Testament also says the spirit of Beliar was troubling her and that Joseph prayed to Yahuah (the Lord) when he saw it. That is the Testament's own telling, since Genesis names no spirit, and the reader should not build on it. Genesis and Proverbs give enough: the pressure, the refusal, and the cords that hold a man who gives way.

chapters.flag: 117:4 names 'the spirit of Beliar' troubling her; Genesis names no such spirit. Set Genesis and Proverbs beside the chapter; nothing built on the line.

cards.note: Genesis 39:3 — *And his master saw that Yahuah (LORD) was with him, and that Yahuah (LORD) made all that he did to prosper in his hand.* *Now, therefore, render justice unto him, and take away the youth to thy house; so shall the Elohim (God) of the Hebrews bless thee, for grace from heaven is upon him.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 122:3) The woman in the Testament of Joseph tells her husband that "grace from heaven is upon" the young Hebrew. Genesis says the same thing about what Potiphar himself saw: that Yahuah (the LORD) was with Joseph and made all he did to prosper.
cards.member_note: Genesis 39:3 — *his master saw that Yahuah (LORD) was with him.* What Potiphar saw in Joseph is what the Testament of Joseph has the Egyptian woman say.

cards.note: Genesis 39:5 — *And it came to pass from the time that he had made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, that Yahuah (LORD) blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake; and the blessing of Yahuah (LORD) was upon all that he had in the house, and in the field.* *Now, therefore, render justice unto him, and take away the youth to thy house; so shall the Elohim (God) of the Hebrews bless thee, for grace from heaven is upon him.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 122:3) The Testament of Joseph has the woman say that the Elohim (God) of the Hebrews would bless her husband for the youth's sake, and Genesis tells that Yahuah (the LORD) blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake. The blessing came as she said, whatever else she was saying it for.
cards.member_note: Genesis 39:5 — *Yahuah (LORD) blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake.* A house is blessed for Joseph's sake, in Genesis and in the Testament of Joseph.

cards.note: Genesis 40:15 — *For indeed I was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews: and here also have I done nothing that they should put me into the dungeon.* *And she told her husband that the merchant had become rich by means of a young Hebrew, and they say that he had assuredly been stolen out of the land of Canaan.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 122:2) Joseph in Genesis says he was "stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews," and the Egyptian woman in the Testament of Joseph says that he was stolen out of the land of Canaan. In both the claim is that this was a captive and not a slave by right.
cards.member_note: Genesis 40:15 — *I was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews.* Joseph was stolen from his own land, as Genesis has him say and the Testament of Joseph has the woman say.

cards.note: Genesis 39:1 — *And Joseph was brought down to Egypt; and Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him of the hands of the Ishmeelites, which had brought him down thither.* *And about that time the Memphian woman, the wife of Pentephri, came down 'in a chariot', 'with great pomp, because she had heard from her eunuchs concerning me'.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 122:1) Genesis tells simply that Potiphar, the captain of the guard, bought Joseph from the Ishmeelites who brought him down. The Testament of Joseph tells of a merchant, a chariot and the woman's eunuchs, which are details of its own, while the buyer and the seller in Genesis stand as the record.
cards.member_note: Genesis 39:1 — *Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him.* Potiphar buys Joseph in Genesis, and the Testament of Joseph tells the buying in more colour.

thread.title: Grace from heaven is upon the Hebrew youth — how Joseph came into Potiphar's house
thread.summary_md:
In the Testament of Joseph the Egyptian woman sets the purchase in motion, hearing of the young Hebrew from her eunuchs and going to her husband, while Genesis tells the same event plainly from the husband's side.

*And about that time the Memphian woman, the wife of Pentephri, came down 'in a chariot', 'with great pomp, because she had heard from her eunuchs concerning me'.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 122:1)

*And Joseph was brought down to Egypt; and Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him of the hands of the Ishmeelites, which had brought him down thither.* (Genesis 39:1)

What she says to him is what Genesis says Potiphar saw for himself, and the blessing she promised came.

*Now, therefore, render justice unto him, and take away the youth to thy house; so shall the Elohim (God) of the Hebrews bless thee, for grace from heaven is upon him.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 122:3)

*And his master saw that Yahuah (LORD) was with him, and that Yahuah (LORD) made all that he did to prosper in his hand.* (Genesis 39:3)

*And it came to pass from the time that he had made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, that Yahuah (LORD) blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake; and the blessing of Yahuah (LORD) was upon all that he had in the house, and in the field.* (Genesis 39:5)

She also says the youth had been stolen out of Canaan, and Joseph said so himself years later.

*And she told her husband that the merchant had become rich by means of a young Hebrew, and they say that he had assuredly been stolen out of the land of Canaan.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 122:2)

*For indeed I was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews: and here also have I done nothing that they should put me into the dungeon.* (Genesis 40:15)

It ain't new that Yahuah (the LORD) was with Joseph in Egypt. Genesis says it again and again, and the Testament lets even an Egyptian say it. The merchant, the chariot and the court scene are the Testament's own telling. Hold the plain scripture: a son of Yashar'el (Israel) stolen from the land of the Hebrews and blessed in a foreign house because Yahuah (the LORD) was with him.

chapters.flag: The chariot, the merchant and the woman's own agency in the purchase (122:1-3) are the Testament's elaboration; Genesis 37:28,36 has Midianites/Ishmeelites selling Joseph to Potiphar.

cards.note: Genesis 37:28 — *Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver: and they brought Joseph into Egypt.* *And he said: How didst thou become their slave? And I said: They bought me out of the land of Canaan.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 123:8) When Joseph says in the Testament of Joseph that "They bought me out of the land of Canaan," he is telling in short what Genesis tells: he was sold to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver and brought into Egypt.
cards.member_note: Genesis 37:28 — *sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver.* Joseph's sale out of Canaan is the plain fact under his answer to Pentephris.

cards.note: Genesis 39:1 — *And Joseph was brought down to Egypt; and Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him of the hands of the Ishmeelites, which had brought him down thither.* *And Pentephris said unto him: Whence, then, is the Hebrew slave? And he said: The Ishmaelites entrusted him to me until they should return.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 123:3) The merchant in the Testament of Joseph says "The Ishmaelites entrusted him to me." Genesis names the Ishmeelites too, as those who brought Joseph down to Egypt and sold him to Potiphar.
cards.member_note: Genesis 39:1 — *bought him of the hands of the Ishmeelites.* The Ishmeelites are the sellers in both the Testament of Joseph and Genesis.

cards.note: Psalm 105:17 — *He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant:* *And he took me apart from him, and said unto me: Art thou a slave or free? And I said: A slave.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 123:6) When Pentephris asks "Art thou a slave or free?" and Joseph answers "A slave," he is saying what the psalm says: he was sold for a servant. The psalm adds that he was a man sent before them, so the selling was also a sending.
cards.member_note: Psalm 105:17 — *He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant.* Joseph answers "a slave" and the psalm says he was sold for a servant.

cards.note: Psalm 105:18 — *Whose feet they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron:* *And he said unto me: 'Truly' thou liest; and 'straightway' he commanded me to be stripped and beaten.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 123:9) The Testament of Joseph tells that Joseph was stripped and beaten for his answer, and the psalm says that his feet were hurt with fetters and he was laid in iron. The suffering is told differently, but both put it on a man who had done nothing.
cards.member_note: Psalm 105:18 — *Whose feet they hurt with fetters.* Joseph's suffering as a slave is told in Psalm 105 and in the Testament of Joseph.

thread.title: Art thou a slave or free? — Joseph is stripped and beaten, and says a slave
thread.summary_md:
The Testament of Joseph lets the reader hear the questioning, with Pentephris asking, the merchant lying and Joseph answering, while Genesis names who really sold him to Potiphar.

*And Pentephris said unto him: Whence, then, is the Hebrew slave? And he said: The Ishmaelites entrusted him to me until they should return.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 123:3)

*And Joseph was brought down to Egypt; and Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him of the hands of the Ishmeelites, which had brought him down thither.* (Genesis 39:1)

Joseph is then asked his own condition, and his answer is short and true, the same as the plain statement in Genesis about how he was sold, which the psalm sums up as a man sold for a servant.

*And he took me apart from him, and said unto me: Art thou a slave or free? And I said: A slave.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 123:6)

*And he said: How didst thou become their slave? And I said: They bought me out of the land of Canaan.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 123:8)

*Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver: and they brought Joseph into Egypt.* (Genesis 37:28)

*He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant:* (Psalm 105:17)

The Testament has him stripped and beaten for the answer, and the psalm remembers what Joseph suffered.

*And he said unto me: 'Truly' thou liest; and 'straightway' he commanded me to be stripped and beaten.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 123:9)

*Whose feet they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron:* (Psalm 105:18)

It ain't new that Joseph was sold and afflicted, since Genesis and Psalm 105 had it already. The Testament dramatizes a scene the older books pass over, and it lets Joseph give the answer that spared his brothers shame. It speaks only of Ishmaelites where Genesis also names Midianites, so Genesis 37:28 remains the record. Genesis does not tell this interview, and the Testament is best read beside the verses above and not in place of them.

chapters.flag: The interrogation scene (merchant, Pentephris, beating) is not in Genesis; set beside Genesis 37, 39 and Psalm 105 only. Genesis 37:28 names Midianites and Ishmeelites together; the Testament names only the Ishmaelites.

cards.note: Genesis 39:20 — *And Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound: and he was there in the prison.* *And when I made no change in my statement, 'though I was beaten', he ordered me to be imprisoned, until, he said, the owners of the boy should come.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 124:2) Joseph in the Testament of Joseph is imprisoned "the owners of the boy should come," and Genesis tells where he was put: the prison, a place where the king's prisoners were bound. The reason the two give is different, but the prison is the same.
cards.member_note: Genesis 39:20 — *put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound* Joseph is shut in the king's prison, in Genesis and in the Testament of Joseph.

cards.note: Genesis 39:7 — *And it came to pass after these things, that his master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph; and she said, Lie with me.* *For she wished to see me out of a desire 'of sin', but I was ignorant concerning all these things.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 124:4) The Testament of Joseph says the woman wished to see him "out of a desire" while Joseph "was ignorant concerning all these things". Genesis gives the same fact in a few words: she cast her eyes upon Joseph and said, Lie with me.
cards.member_note: Genesis 39:7 — *his master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph.* Her desire for Joseph begins with a look, in Genesis and in the Testament of Joseph.

cards.note: Psalm 105:19 — *Until the time that his word came: the word of Yahuah (LORD) tried him.* *And when I made no change in my statement, 'though I was beaten', he ordered me to be imprisoned, until, he said, the owners of the boy should come.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 124:2) In the Testament of Joseph, Joseph sticks to his story though beaten and is imprisoned. The psalm says what the prison was for: until the time that his word came, the word of Yahuah (the LORD) tried him.
cards.member_note: Psalm 105:19 — *the word of Yahuah (LORD) tried him.* The prison tested Joseph, as the psalm says of this season of his life.

thread.title: The well-born captive in bonds — Joseph imprisoned, and the word that tried him
thread.summary_md:
In the Testament of Joseph the woman watches the beating from her window and pleads that the lad be set free, but Joseph does not change his word and is thrown into prison, a place Genesis also names.

*And when I made no change in my statement, 'though I was beaten', he ordered me to be imprisoned, until, he said, the owners of the boy should come.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 124:2)

*And Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound: and he was there in the prison.* (Genesis 39:20)

The Testament is plain about her reason for pleading for him, and Genesis states it at the start, when her desire first appeared.

*For she wished to see me out of a desire 'of sin', but I was ignorant concerning all these things.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 124:4)

*And it came to pass after these things, that his master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph; and she said, Lie with me.* (Genesis 39:7)

It ain't new that Joseph was shut up in the king's prison. What the psalm adds is that the prison was a testing, and the Testament of Joseph shows what the testing looked like on the day it began, a beating, a prison, and a lad who did not alter what he said.

*Until the time that his word came: the word of Yahuah (LORD) tried him.* (Psalm 105:19)

The Testament and Genesis differ on how Joseph came to the prison. Genesis puts it after the woman's false charge, when she called the men of her house and accused him, while the Testament has the prison come first, on the husband's doubt about the youth's status, and the reader should see this as the Testament's own account of the same affliction. What holds in both is that a son of Yashar'el (Israel) was bound without cause and that Yahuah (the LORD) was with him there.

chapters.flag: The court scene (window, husband's reply, prison pending the owners) differs from Genesis 39, where Joseph is jailed after the false accusation (39:14-20). Summary says so; no attempt to harmonize.

cards.note: Proverbs 12:16 — *A fool’s wrath is presently known: but a prudent man covereth shame.* *And though I knew (this) I held my peace, lest the eunuch should be put to shame.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 126:6) Joseph in the Testament of Joseph knew the eunuch had cheated him on the price, and "held my peace, lest the eunuch should be put to shame." Proverbs calls that kind of silence prudence, a prudent man covers shame while a fool's wrath is known at once.
cards.member_note: Proverbs 12:16 — *A fool’s wrath is presently known: but a prudent man covereth shame.* Joseph's silence about the eunuch's lie is the prudence Proverbs describes.

cards.note: Genesis 37:36 — *And the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh’s, and captain of the guard.* *And 'straightway' she sent a eunuch to the Ishmaelites, and asked them to sell me.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 126:2) The Testament of Joseph has the woman send a eunuch to the Ishmaelites to buy Joseph. Genesis closes the chapter of his sale with Joseph already sold into Egypt to Potiphar, the captain of the guard.
cards.member_note: Genesis 37:36 — *the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar.* Joseph is sold on to Potiphar, as Genesis says, though the Testament of Joseph tells of the buying differently.

cards.note: Genesis 37:28 — *Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver: and they brought Joseph into Egypt.* *The eunuch therefore went and gave them eighty pieces of gold, and 'he received me'; but to the Egyptian woman he said: I have given a hundred.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 126:5) The eunuch in the Testament of Joseph "gave them eighty pieces of gold" and told his mistress it was a hundred. Genesis says the first price, when Joseph was sold to the Ishmeelites, was twenty pieces of silver. The sums differ, and the Testament should be read as a separate telling.
cards.member_note: Genesis 37:28 — *sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver* What Joseph was sold for in Genesis is the price of the first sale; the Testament of Joseph tells of a second.

thread.title: I knew it and held my peace — Joseph covers the eunuch's shame
thread.summary_md:
The Testament of Joseph tells the buying of Joseph from the Egyptian side, with the woman's eunuchs going back and forth to the Ishmaelites, until the youth comes into her house for a price and the eunuch keeps part of it for himself.

*The eunuch therefore went and gave them eighty pieces of gold, and 'he received me'; but to the Egyptian woman he said: I have given a hundred.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 126:5)

Genesis counts the first sale in silver and names the sellers who passed by, and it tells the sale into Potiphar's house in a single verse.

*Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver: and they brought Joseph into Egypt.* (Genesis 37:28)

*And the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh’s, and captain of the guard.* (Genesis 37:36)

Joseph says in the Testament what he did when he knew the eunuch had cheated, and Proverbs names that restraint for what it is.

*And though I knew (this) I held my peace, lest the eunuch should be put to shame.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 126:6)

*A fool’s wrath is presently known: but a prudent man covereth shame.* (Proverbs 12:16)

It ain't new that a righteous man will keep another's shame hidden rather than take his own advantage. Proverbs had the saying, and the Testament shows a young slave living it before he had any power at all. The details differ from Genesis, which speaks of Midianites and Ishmeelites, twenty pieces of silver and a sale to Potiphar, where the Testament speaks of a mistress, eunuchs, minae and gold, so the two should be kept apart. The value of the passage is that it shows Joseph, a son of Yashar'el (Israel), covering a stranger's fault while he himself was being sold.

chapters.flag: The eunuch/price episode (126:2-6) is the Testament's elaboration; it does not fit Genesis 37:28,36 and 39:1 without harmonizing, which is not attempted. 'Minae' and 'gold' are the Testament's, Genesis has silver.
